narrative:
The model predicted a 75% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also worked against you, landing in the fifth decile compared with an average of sixth among those who were accepted. These two performance measures together signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in your favor. At 41, it sits above the 37.2 average of accepted applicants and therefore pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the concerns raised by your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way. Your family income, undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time were also far less important to this particular decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the bar exam preparation courses or seeking additional support in the areas where your decile rankings were lower. Raising those class standings in future semesters or through supplemental study could meaningfully change how a similar model evaluates your profile.
